consensus_summary: Mainstream Christian readings treat the new moon chiefly as an OT ceremonial/appointed-time observance, typically grouped with festivals and sabbaths, whose typological meaning is a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17), with secondary associations of renewal, empty ritual when divorced from faithfulness, and eschatological ongoing worship.
book_summary: The book defines the new moon as the renewed moon—specifically the full moon in the east gate—that marks the start of the month and serves as the sign of the appointed times, contrasting the common conjunction/first-crescent view.
consensus_core_identification: Monthly ceremonial appointed time / shadow whose substance is Christ (with renewal as a common secondary sense).
book_core_identification: The full (renewed) moon in the east gate as the phase that begins the month and signs the appointed times.
boundary_disagreement: Consensus does not identify which lunar phase counts as the biblical new moon; the book restricts the referent to the full moon at the east gate and excludes the dark conjunction and first visible crescent commonly assumed as month-start.
material_contradiction: None at the consensus core: the book’s full-moon calendrical identification is not a stated consensus claim to contradict, but an absent specialized referent.
rationale: Reduced cores differ in kind. Blind consensus centers theological/typological meaning of the known monthly observance (shadow in Christ, renewal, critique of empty rite, eschatological worship). The book’s lead identification is astronomical-calendrical: new moon = full/renewed moon in the east gate as month-start and moed sign. No consensus primary or listed alternative covers that full-moon/east-gate identification, so the relation is novelty (absence), not equivalent wording, boundary refinement of the same core, or direct replacement of the shadow/renewal core.
strongest_objection: Printed texts establish new-moon observance, east-gate opening, and shadow language but do not by themselves entail that the biblical new moon is the full moon rather than conjunction or crescent.
